history.text: In Eritrea, the Afar are one of at least four Indigenous peoples, who have lived in their traditional territories for about two thousand years.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Eritrea chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

context.text: Ethiopia's Afar State is home to about 1.8 million Afar people, by a government projection.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Eritrea chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

context.text: In 2008 Afar pastoralists set up the Afar Pastoralist Council so they could raise their voices at regional, national and international level.

source.title: Afar Pastoralist Council holds Inaugural General Meeting

history.text: The Mosopisyek Benet have lived on Mount Elgon in Uganda for more than five hundred years.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Uganda chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

context.text: In May 2023 Uganda's Office of the Prime Minister directed the wildlife authority (UWA) to stop evictions of Benet communities.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, Uganda chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

context.text: In 2005 Uganda's High Court recognized the Benet as the historical, indigenous inhabitants of Mount Elgon, a landmark land-rights ruling.

source.title: Momentous Ruling Recognizes Land Rights of Indigenous Community

history.text: Klaarwater, the settlement Griqua people founded, later took the name Griquatown.

context.text: Early Griqua communities governed themselves through leaders called kaptyns, with magistrates drawn from leading families.
Griqua communities live today in the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Northern Cape, Free State and KwaZulu-Natal.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, South Africa chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

history.text: The Mbuti, with the Baka and Batwa, are widely acknowledged as the first inhabitants of the DR Congo's rainforests.

source.title: The Indigenous World 2024, DRC chapter (IWGIA yearbook PDF)
source.publisher: IWGIA (International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs)

context.text: Mbuti and Efe peoples live in the Okapi Wildlife Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Ituri forest, which is essential to their economy and culture.
UNESCO calls for ensuring the involvement of the Indigenous Mbuti and Efe peoples in the management of the Okapi Wildlife Reserve.

history.text: Alutiiq/Sugpiaq people have lived along the coasts of south-central Alaska for more than 7,800 years and descend from seafaring ancestors.

context.text: At the Alutiiq Museum, fluent speakers, learners and linguists work together to record Sugt'stun and teach it to a new generation of speakers.
Sugpiaq, the people's traditional name for themselves, joins suk, meaning person, with piaq, meaning real.

source.title: Languages - Alutiiq / Sugpiaq
source.publisher: Alaska Native Language Center, University of Alaska Fairbanks

history.text: People have lived in American Samoa for more than 3,000 years, making it one of Polynesia's oldest places of human settlement.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

context.text: In American Samoa, land is held communally under the guidance of village chiefs, the matai, and the national park there sits on land leased from local villages.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

context.text: Fa'asamoa, the Samoan way of life, took shape over many centuries and remains the base of Samoan identity and everyday living.

source.title: History & Culture
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, National Park of American Samoa

history.text: In 2001 Funai, Brazil's Indigenous affairs agency, officially recognized the Tupinambá of Olivença as an Indigenous people.

context.text: The Tupinambá of Olivença live in the Atlantic Forest region of southern Bahia.

history.text: Since the late 1980s, supported by neighboring Sierra Nevada peoples, the Kankuamo have led a process of cultural renewal and peaceful resistance.

source.title: Kankuamos, guardianes del equilibrio del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

context.text: In 2022 UNESCO recognized the ancestral knowledge system shared by the Kankuamo, Arhuaco, Kogui and Wiwa as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
The Kankuamo resguardo, about 24,212 hectares near Valledupar, was collectively titled to the people in 2003.

source.title: Kankuamos, guardianes del equilibrio del mundo
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

history.text: Yanacona leader Juan Gregorio Palechor, of the Guachicono resguardo, was among the community leaders who formed the CRIC in Cauca in 1971.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

context.text: The Yanacona are recovering their identity and culture, including their traditional language, Quechua, and strengthening their cabildo authorities.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

context.text: Yanacona territory covers a large part of the Macizo Colombiano, the mountain region of southern Cauca.

source.title: Los Yanacona, reconstruyendo la casa
source.publisher: Ministerio de Cultura de Colombia, Dirección de Poblaciones

history.text: The Dolgan formed as a people in the north of the Yenisei region between the 17th and 19th centuries and took final shape in the early 20th century.

source.title: Долганы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

context.text: During an August 2026 folk culture expedition to Khatanga, the Dolgan dried-fish dish kerdiileek was added to the list of Taimyr's intangible cultural heritage.

source.title: Долганская юкола «кэрдиилээк» признана объектом нематериального наследия Таймыра
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

context.text: Dolgan is a Turkic language, close to Sakha (Yakut), from which it separated through isolated development.

source.title: Долганы
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

history.text: Arctic explorers relied on Inughuit skill and knowledge of the far north to succeed, and Inughuit elders later shared their knowledge to help a US museum document that history.

source.title: This Extraordinary Paradise: Living in Northwest Greenland

context.text: The Inughuit have their own language, or dialect, and a hunting culture that is distinctive in several ways.
Hunting is still a significant part of the livelihood of several families in Qaanaaq, Greenland's youngest and northernmost town.

history.text: Chukchi have used pictographs since ancient times, and their oldest known documents are inscribed walrus tusks.

source.title: The Chukchis
source.publisher: The Red Book of the Peoples of the Russian Empire (Institute of the Estonian Language archive)

context.text: Researchers at Russia's Kunstkamera museum published a 2018 study on the mobile dwellings of Chukchi reindeer herders, covering both traditions and innovations.

source.title: Arctic Research Center
source.publisher: Peter the Great Museum of Anthropology and Ethnography (Kunstkamera), Russian Academy of Sciences

context.text: Carving bone and walrus ivory and embroidering with reindeer hair are long-standing Chukchi arts, practised alongside reindeer herding and hunting.

source.title: Чукчи
source.publisher: RAIPON (Association of Indigenous Small-Numbered Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East)

history.text: Historically, every Mizo village had its own chief, who was assisted by a council of elders.

context.text: Mizoram became a full state of India on 20 February 1987; its Legislative Assembly first met on 10 May 1972.

history.text: Orang Asli were collectors and primary traders in the peninsula's economy as early as the 5th century CE.

context.text: Orang Asli, a Malay collective term meaning original or first peoples, covers 18 officially listed groups of Peninsular Malaysia.
The Orang Asli are not one group: each people has its own language and culture and sees itself as distinct.
Some Temuan, Jakun and Semai families now run their own rubber, oil palm or cocoa farms.

history.text: In Tao migration history, the ancestors lived on the Batanes islands of the northern Philippines before settling on Lanyu.

context.text: The Tao, who live on Lanyu, also called Orchid Island, numbered 4,684 in January 2020.
The people call themselves Tao, meaning human, while Yami is the name used officially.

history.text: Thao oral history tells of ancestors who followed a white deer to Sun Moon Lake and found a fertile place full of fish.

context.text: Thao people live mainly in Ita Thao Village in Yuchi Township and in Dapinglin, Shuili Township, both in Nantou County. They numbered about 817 in January 2020.

history.text: In 1949 the Nation set up the Union of Ontario Indians as its secretariat, replacing the Grand General Indian Council, which first met under that name in 1870.

context.text: The Anishinabek Nation speaks for 39 First Nations in Ontario with about 70,000 citizens, roughly one third of the province's First Nation population.
It is Ontario's oldest political organization, with roots in the Confederacy of Three Fires that long predates European contact.

history.text: In 1997 the Supreme Court of Canada, in R. v. Gladstone, recognized a Heiltsuk Aboriginal right to harvest and sell herring spawn on kelp.

context.text: In 2025 Heiltsuk members ratified a written constitution, a milestone in self-governance.
Haíɫzaqv means 'to speak and act correctly', principles that guide Heiltsuk ancestral and present-day ways of life.

history.text: Signed on June 5, 1984, the Inuvialuit Final Agreement was the first comprehensive land claim agreement north of 60 degrees latitude, and only the second in Canada at the time.

context.text: Six communities lie within the Inuvialuit Settlement Region: Aklavik, Inuvik, Paulatuk, Sachs Harbour, Tuktoyaktuk and Ulukhaktok.
One of the agreement's basic goals is keeping Inuvialuit cultural identity and values strong as northern society changes.

history.text: Ktunaxa people have lived beside the Kootenay and Columbia Rivers and the Arrow Lakes for more than 10,000 years.

context.text: The Ktunaxa Nation Council helps represent the shared interests of four Ktunaxa First Nations within ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the Ktunaxa homelands.
ʔamakʔis Ktunaxa, the traditional territory, covers about 70,000 square kilometres in the Kootenay region of southeastern British Columbia.

history.text: In 1999 the Marshall decision of the Supreme Court of Canada recognized the Treaties of 1760 and 1761, along with a right to hunt, fish and gather to earn a moderate livelihood.

context.text: Mi'kmaw communities in Nova Scotia wrote their own Netukulimk Livelihood Management Plans so members who fish can support themselves and their families.
In 2006 the 13 Mi'kmaw Chiefs of Nova Scotia formed the Assembly of Nova Scotia Mi'kmaw Chiefs to guide the Nation's negotiators on rights and title.

history.text: Treaty 7 was signed in 1877 at Blackfoot Crossing, on Siksika land.

context.text: Siksika Nation has about 7,800 members, and its language is Siksika, or Blackfoot.
Siksika's coat of arms, registered with the Canadian Heraldic Authority in June 1992, was the first registered by any Nation in Canada.

history.text: In 1846 the border that now divides Canada and the United States was drawn across Syilx territory without the Nation's consent, separating lands and families.

context.text: Historically the Okanagan Nation Alliance represented eight member communities: seven in Canada and the Colville Confederated Tribes in Washington State.
The Okanagan Nation Alliance reports that the new Okanagan Dam Fish Passage, after years of advocacy and planning, lets salmon reach Okanagan Lake for the first time in nearly 100 years.

history.text: The Supreme Court of Canada has ruled that the Peace and Friendship Treaties remain legally binding, and they are the foundation of Wolastoqey treaty rights.

context.text: Six Wolastoqey communities in New Brunswick, Matawaskiye, Neqotkuk, Pilick, Sitansisk, Welamukotuk and Wotstak, work together through the Wolastoqey Nation in New Brunswick.
The Wolastoqiyik are the people of the Wolastoq watershed, a homeland of land, sea and fresh water reaching from the Bay of Fundy to the St. Lawrence River.

history.text: Guna authors note that their self-government existed long before any state law recognized it; Panama's Law 16 of 1953 legally organized the comarca now called Gunayala.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

context.text: Gunayala's 49 communities govern themselves together through the Guna General Congress, their highest political and administrative body for land, resources and education.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

context.text: Gunayala runs along Panama's Caribbean coast to the Colombian border, with about 315 km of coastline and over 400 small islands and islets.

source.title: Gunayala: A Living Model of Autonomy and Self-government

history.text: An 1882 border treaty between Mexico and Guatemala left the Mam people divided between the two countries.

source.title: Mames : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

context.text: In October 2025, the Mam communities of Cajolá and Todos Santos Cuchumatán joined two other Maya communities in reporting to a UN committee on their community radio rights.

source.title: Indigenous Communities and Cultural Survival Urge CERD to Address Community Radio Rights Violations in Guatemala

context.text: B'alam Stereo in Cabricán, among the longer-running Indigenous stations in Guatemala's highlands, has served the Maya Mam since 1976, with work promoting education, health, water and justice.

source.title: Announcing Our 2019 Community Media Grants Partners

context.text: Mam crafts vary by community and include baskets, pottery, wool mantillones, palm hats, wooden toys and decorated gourds.

source.title: Mames : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

history.text: In 2014 El Salvador amended article 63 of its constitution to recognize Indigenous Peoples and commit to policies supporting their identity and culture.

source.title: The Resilience and Resistance of the Nahuat Pipil Peoples of El Salvador

context.text: In Santo Domingo de Guzmán, Nahuat-speaking teachers created Nahuatl cribs where children learn the language, and Radio Sensunat promotes Nahuat Pipil culture.

source.title: Radio Sensunat: Broadcasting to Revitalize the Nahuat Language in El Salvador

context.text: Izalco is the only municipality in El Salvador with an ancestral Indigenous government, made up of mayordomos and mayordomas.

source.title: Radio Sensunat: Broadcasting to Revitalize the Nahuat Language in El Salvador

history.text: Traces of Chatino culture in the coastal zone of Oaxaca date back to around 400 BCE.

source.title: Chatinos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

context.text: Since 1994, La Voz de la Costa Chica in Santiago Jamiltepec, Oaxaca has broadcast in Mixtec, Amuzgo, Chatino, Tacuate and Spanish.

source.title: XEJAM La Voz de la Costa Chica (AM) : Radio cultural indígena México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), with station information from INPI

context.text: Chatino weaving and embroidery continue in Yaitepec, Quiahije and Nopala, where blouses, shoulder bags, sashes and tablecloths are made.

source.title: Chatinos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

history.text: Amuzgo oral history says the people came from the sea, from islands they call ndyuaa xenncue, the lands in the middle.

source.title: Amuzgos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

context.text: After a struggle that began in 1920, Amuzgo lands were restored as an ejido on August 25, 1933, covering 6,384 hectares.

source.title: Amuzgos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

context.text: Amuzgo women weave huipiles, rebozos and tablecloths on the backstrap loom, while men make bamboo and palm baskets.

source.title: Amuzgos : Pueblos indígenas México : Sistema de Información Cultural-Secretaría de Cultura
source.publisher: Secretaría de Cultura, Sistema de Información Cultural (SIC), Gobierno de México

history.text: For about the last 300 years most Zuni people have lived in one main village, the Pueblo of Zuni, with farming villages used at planting and harvest.

context.text: The Pueblo of Zuni counts about 18,692 people and holds about 463,287 acres of reservation land.

history.text: Archaeologists agree that Acoma has been lived in continuously since at least AD 1200, and Acoma oral history reaches back much further.

context.text: Since 2017 the Acoma Language Program has been building a Keres dictionary, with about 5,000 words and phrases being edited by fluent speakers.
In 1999 Acoma set up a Historic Preservation Office to keep traditional skills alive, among them stone cutting, wood carving, pottery making and weaving.

history.text: In 1859 Congress created the first reservation in Arizona along the Gila River, in appreciation of the Akimel O’otham role in westward travel.

context.text: The Akimel O’otham welcomed the Pee Posh (Maricopa) to the Gila River long ago, and the two peoples still share its lands and resources today.
Akimel O’otham basket weaving is in revival, and in 2004 the community dedicated the Huhugam Heritage Center to care for its heritage.

history.text: The Cocopah, known as the River People, have lived along the lower Colorado River and its delta for centuries.

context.text: About 1,000 Cocopah tribal members live and work on or near their reservation south of Yuma, Arizona, which was established in 1917.
Since 2003 the Cucapá of El Mayor, Baja California, and the Cocopah of Somerton, Arizona, have met each year with dances, songs, crafts and food.

source.title: Cucapás
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

history.text: The Havasu Baaja, People of the Blue Green Waters, have made the village of Supai below the Grand Canyon rim their home for over 1,000 years.

context.text: Supai is so remote that the US Postal Service carries all mail in and out of the canyon by mule train.
The Havasupai reservation was set up in 1880 and greatly enlarged in 1975. It covers 188,077 acres beside the South Rim of the Grand Canyon.

history.text: Chiricahua Apache families arrived at the Mescalero reservation in 1913 after imprisonment at Fort Sill, Oklahoma.

context.text: Today three peoples, the Mescalero, Lipan and Chiricahua Apache, together make up the Mescalero Apache Tribe on a 463,000 acre reservation.
The Mescalero Apache Tribe owns and runs the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and the Ski Apache ski area.

source.title: Official Website of the Mescalero Apache Tribe

context.text: The Tribe is governed by an eight member Tribal Council with an elected President and Vice-President, each chosen by secret ballot for two years.

history.text: The people have long called their home Ohkay Owingeh, place of the strong people in Tewa, and officially restored that name in place of San Juan, given in 1598.
People have lived at Ohkay Owingeh since about AD 1200, farming with irrigation along the Rio Grande.

context.text: Ohkay Owingeh is the headquarters of the Eight Northern Pueblo Tribal Council.

history.text: From the 1700s to today the Rarámuri have practiced a quiet resistance, and some moved to remote parts of the sierra to keep their traditions.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

context.text: Rarámuri artisans make violins, drums, palm baskets, clay pots and wooden masks, and sell them in towns such as Guachochi, Creel and Batopilas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

context.text: The Rarámuri ball race is a contest in which runners cover long distances while kicking a wooden ball, and it is held as part of community fiestas.

source.title: Tarahumaras
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

history.text: In colonial times the people formed two branches, one in Chihuahua influenced by the Rarámuri and one in Sonora influenced by the Yoreme.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

context.text: Warihó and Macurawe families weave baskets, mats and hats from palm and fiber and build harps, violins and guitars. Their craft work is family based and rests with women.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

context.text: The people call themselves Macurawe in Sonora and Warihó in Chihuahua. Their Uto-Aztecan language has two variants and bridges Tarahumara and Mayo.

source.title: Guarijíos
source.publisher: Sistema de Información Cultural, Secretaría de Cultura (Mexico)

history.text: The Tribe recounts that by 1880, Lipan communities lived along the Rio Grande on both sides of the United States-Mexico border.

context.text: In 2021, the City and County of Presidio donated a Lipan cemetery parcel to the Lipan Apache Tribe.

source.title: El Cementerio de los Lipanes Transferred to Tribe

context.text: The Lipan Apache Tribe in Texas maintains a Tribal Council responsible for community welfare and protection of its heritage.

history.text: Southern Ute government is based on a constitution adopted in 1936 and revised in 1975.

context.text: The Tribe's Brunot Area guide explains the hunting right reserved in the 1873 agreement, despite the loss of reservation lands.
The Southern Ute Indian Tribe is made up of the Mouache and Caputa bands and is headquartered in Ignacio, Colorado.
An elected Tribal Council governs the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, which maintains its own constitution, laws and tribal courts.

history.text: In 1875, Tonto and Yavapai people were forcibly moved from the Rio Verde Reserve to San Carlos. Some Tonto families later returned to Payson.

context.text: In 2010, land for the Tonto Apache Tribe was acquired in trust following a land exchange with the U.S. Forest Service.

source.title: Reservation proclamation for trust land belonging to the Tonto Apache Tribe of Arizona

context.text: The Tonto Apache Tribe is based beside Payson in northwestern Gila County, Arizona.

history.text: In 1881, the United States forcibly removed White River Utes from Colorado to the Uintah Reservation.

source.title: Ute Indians
source.publisher: Utah Division of State History, History to Go

context.text: In an April 2026 statement, the Ute Indian Tribe announced it would appeal a federal district court decision concerning split-estate reservation lands.

source.title: Tribe will appeal Utah Federal District Court decision on split estate lands

context.text: The Ute Indian Tribe elects Business Committee representatives from the Uintah, Uncompahgre and Whiteriver bands.
The Tribe delegates protection, restoration and management of Uintah and Ouray Reservation water resources to its Water Resources Department and Commission.

history.text: The Weenuche Band organized a tribal government and adopted a constitution six years after the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934.

context.text: The Ute Mountain Ute Tribe identifies itself as the Weenuche band of the Ute Nation, with its tribal offices in Towaoc, Colorado.
White Mesa Administration supports community members with employment, education and access to basic services in White Mesa, Utah.
The Ute Mountain Ute Tribal Council is elected by the tribal membership and governs the reservation.

history.text: The Mahkontowe pihlengfong, a Kosraean night story, tells how the Tokosra's seat of political power moved from Likinlulem to Lelu Island, home of the Lelu Ruins.

context.text: In 2017 Kosraean elders proposed protecting Kosrae's mountain range, seen as the figure Mahkontowe, now the Mahkontowe Conservation Area under Kosrae State law.
Kosrae State has its own constitutional government, with a legislature elected by voters in the districts of Lelu, Malem, Tafunsak and Utwe.

source.title: Kosrae
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

history.text: Nan Madol's more than 100 islets off south-east Pohnpei hold the remains of stone palaces, temples and residences built between 1200 and 1500 CE.

source.title: Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia

context.text: Nan Madol, a World Heritage site since 2016, is traditionally owned and managed under the Nahnmwarki system, a chiefly institution that continues in Pohnpei today.

source.title: Nan Madol: Ceremonial Centre of Eastern Micronesia

context.text: Pohnpei State's constitution protects the customs and traditions of Pohnpei's traditional kingdoms alongside its elected government.

source.title: Pohnpei
source.publisher: Legal Information System of the Federated States of Micronesia

history.text: Rapa Nui is the Indigenous name of Easter Island, whose Polynesian society built shrines and raised the stone figures called moai from the 10th to the 16th century.

context.text: Tapati Rapa Nui, the island's main cultural festival, filled two weeks of February 2026 with ancestral competitions, arts and celebrations of Rapa Nui identity, language and traditions.

source.title: Ministra de las Culturas participa en inauguración de la Tapati Rapanui y desarrolla agenda de trabajo en la isla
source.publisher: Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y el Patrimonio (Chile)

context.text: In 2017 Chile handed administration of Rapa Nui National Park to the Rapa Nui people, through the Ma'u Henua indigenous community, for 50 renewable years.

source.title: Presidenta Bachelet entrega administración del Parque Nacional Rapa Nui a la comunidad de Isla de Pascua
source.publisher: Ministerio del Interior y Seguridad Pública, Gobierno de Chile

context.text: In the Tapati's Takona contest, competitors paint their faces and bodies with natural pigments and explain the meaning of their designs to the community.

source.title: Rapa Nui
source.publisher: Memoria Chilena, Biblioteca Nacional de Chile

history.text: Signed in 1794, the Treaty of Canandaigua made peace between the Haudenosaunee and the United States, and it remains in force today.

context.text: Every citizen of the Cayuga Nation belongs to one of the Nation's five clans.
After more than 200 years away, Cayuga Nation citizens once again live on their ancestral homeland in New York's Finger Lakes region.

history.text: On September 17, 1778, Delaware people signed the first Indian treaty with the newly formed United States.

source.title: About Us - Delaware Tribe of Indians

context.text: The Tribe's online Lenape Talking Dictionary holds about 15,380 words, along with recorded stories and songs, and is still growing.

source.title: Language Revitalization - Delaware Tribe of Indians

context.text: The Delaware Tribe of Indians is a federally recognized tribe of the Lenape people, headquartered in Bartlesville, Oklahoma.

history.text: The Seminole Tribe of Florida describes itself as the only tribe in America that never signed a peace treaty.

context.text: Adding the Tampa and Immokalee reservations brought the Seminole Tribe of Florida's federal trust lands to more than 90,000 acres.
The Tribal Council, with a Chairman, a Vice-Chairman and representatives from each reservation, is the chief governing body of the Seminole Tribe of Florida.

history.text: Shinnecock people have lived on Long Island for about 13,000 years, were master whalers, and keep their history and culture very much alive today.

context.text: The Shinnecock Indian Nation has over 1,589 enrolled tribal members.
On October 1, 2010, the Shinnecock Indian Nation was formally recognized by the United States as the 565th federally recognized tribe.

history.text: In 1998 the town of Gay Head returned to its former Wampanoag name, Aquinnah.
Ancestors of the Wampanoag people have lived at Aquinnah for at least 10,000 years, as the first people of Noepe, now Martha's Vineyard.

context.text: The Aquinnah Wampanoag care for 477 acres of their ancestral lands on Martha's Vineyard.

history.text: The Tribe's historical account records an elected Chief and Tribal Governing Council in May 2002.

source.title: Ethno-Historical / Current Snapshot of the Cheroenhaka (Nottoway) Indian Nation of Southhampton County, Virginia

context.text: The Tribe's language page publishes a vocabulary drawn from materials dating to March 4, 1820.
Cheroenhaka (Nottoway) Indian Tribe is based in Southampton County, Virginia.
The Tribe describes Cattashowrock Town's trails as using Iroquoian and English signs to identify local plants and animals.

history.text: According to the Tribe's history, Edy Turner petitioned the Virginia General Assembly on behalf of her people in 1821.

source.title: Tribal History - Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia

context.text: The Tribe says its Community House & Interpretive Center formally opened in Capron on May 5, 2012.

source.title: Community House & Interpretive Center - Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia

context.text: The Tribe's history describes the Nottoway as Iroquoian speakers of southeastern Virginia.

source.title: Tribal History - Nottoway Indian Tribe of Virginia

history.text: The Nation's history describes fishing, oyster harvesting, hunting and farming in settlements on both sides of the Nansemond River.

context.text: The Nation's history dates formal organization with elected officers to 1984.
The Nation's published Environmental Program describes oyster restoration, invasive plant removal and native plant restoration.
